editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech partly answers the question this publication asked last week: what would make the Prime Minister's offer to Holyrood more than a speech? There is now one concrete item. Andy Burnham offered 'DWP devolution', meaning a localised employment-support model shaped by Holyrood. He also said the UK is looking at devolving innovation, enterprise and employability funding. These are real Whitehall levers, not exhortations, and they go to the National Economic Council in a few weeks.

The speech also carries an implicit threat. Burnham warns that Scottish towns could become 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up', and says Holyrood's own local-government reform must 'move faster'. That turns English devolution into a competitive benchmark Edinburgh will be measured against. It is shrewd politics, but it is hard to square with 'problem-solving, not point-scoring'.

There is a harder question the speech skips. His most striking statistic is a seven-year life-expectancy gap between East Renfrewshire and Glasgow, ten miles apart. Those places sit side by side in the same city region. Handing power to regions does not by itself close gaps within a region. That needs the person-by-person approach he praises in Easterhouse, which is slow, costly and hard to scale.

The 'names not numbers' principle is worth applying to his own government first. One in six young Scots is not in education, employment or training, and Burnham rejects 'another top-down scheme designed in the centre'. Yet the government's flagship rail youth offer is a centrally set quota of up to 600 apprentices over four years. If bottom-up support really is the answer to youth worklessness, it should shape England's programmes too, not only the terms offered to Scotland.
